title: Steam Engines and Hopping Machines
summary: After Cayley, inventors tried to make airplanes fly with big, hot, puffing steam engines. Some machines hopped a little way off the ground, one giant machine broke its own rails, and a model plane flew nearly a kilometre over a river. But nobody could steer them yet!

sections.heading: The Airliner That Was Only a Picture
paragraphs: Imagine opening a newspaper in London in 1843 and seeing a picture of a huge, graceful flying machine soaring over the pyramids of Egypt. Its long, straight wings stretch out like a giant seagull's. Two propellers spin behind the wing. A tidy cabin for passengers hangs underneath. The caption promises that soon you will be able to fly to faraway lands in comfort. It looks amazingly like a modern airplane. There is only one problem. It does not exist.

This was the 'Aerial Steam Carriage', nicknamed the Ariel. It was the dream of two men from the small town of Chard in Somerset, in the south-west of England. William Samuel Henson, born in 1812, was an engineer who worked in the local lace-making industry. His friend John Stringfellow, born in 1799 in Sheffield, had also come to Chard to work in lace-making, building the delicate bobbins and carriages used in lace machines. Lace machines needed precise, light, cleverly made parts, which turned out to be excellent training for building flying machines.

Henson and Stringfellow had studied Sir George Cayley's ideas, and their design followed his plan closely: a fixed wing for lift, propellers for thrust, and a tail for stability and steering. Henson received a British patent for it, number 9478, in 1842. The design was enormous for its time. It was to have a wingspan of about 46 metres (150 feet), wider than the wings of many modern airliners, and it was meant to weigh about 1,400 kilograms (3,000 pounds). A specially designed lightweight steam engine of about 50 horsepower was supposed to drive the two propellers. It had a three-wheeled undercarriage, like a modern plane, and it was meant to take off by rolling down a sloping ramp. Henson and Stringfellow hoped it would fly at about 80 km/h (50 mph) and carry 10 to 12 passengers as far as 1,600 kilometres (1,000 miles).

In 1843 the two inventors, along with two business partners named Frederick Marriott and D. E. Colombine, set up the Aerial Transit Company. Its plan, according to the patent, was to carry 'letters, goods and passengers from place to place through the air'. To attract money from investors and support from Parliament, the company launched one of the first big advertising campaigns in aviation history. Artists produced beautiful prints of the Ariel flying over London, over the Nile, over India and over China. The pictures were copied in newspapers and magazines and sold as posters. People talked about the Ariel everywhere.

Not everyone was impressed. Some newspapers laughed at the idea or suggested the whole thing was a hoax or a trick to get money. Investors stayed away. And the hard truth was that the Ariel could never have flown. A 50-horsepower steam engine, with its boiler, water and fuel, was nowhere near powerful enough for a machine that large and heavy. The full-size Ariel was never built.

Still, the Ariel was important. It was the first detailed design for a propeller-driven airplane with a fixed wing, and it showed the world what an airliner might one day look like. Its pictures spread the idea of airplanes far and wide, even though the real machine stayed on paper. Many years later, when London's main airport opened its first purpose-built hotel, it was named 'The Ariel' in honour of the dream from Chard.

sections.heading: Thirty Yards in a Lace Factory
paragraphs: Henson and Stringfellow did not just draw pictures. Between 1844 and 1847 they built and tested models, including one with a wingspan of about 6 metres (20 feet), driven by small steam engines. The tests were disappointing. The models would not fly on their own; at best one made a tentative hop off the wire that guided it. Henson eventually lost heart, married, and later emigrated to the United States, leaving aviation behind.

Stringfellow kept going. In 1848 he built a smaller model, a monoplane with a wingspan of about 3 metres (10 feet), powered by a tiny steam engine he had made himself. He tested it inside a disused lace factory in Chard, where the long, empty rooms gave him space and kept the wind out. On the first attempt the model ran along a guide wire, then flew about 3 metres before it became unstable and crashed, damaging itself.

Stringfellow repaired it and tried again. This time the model left its guide wire and flew freely. According to the accounts, it flew for about 30 yards (roughly 27 metres) in straight, level, powered flight. Thirty yards is not very far, about the length of three buses. But many historians count it as one of the first times an engine-driven, heavier-than-air model flew under its own power, rather than simply gliding downward.

It is worth thinking about why this tiny model could fly when the giant Ariel could not. There is a simple rule of size: when you make something bigger, its weight grows much faster than the area of its wings. A model that is twice as long, twice as wide and twice as tall weighs about eight times as much, but has only about four times as much wing area. So small models can fly with weak engines, while full-size machines need far more power for every kilogram. This 'square-cube' problem would trip up inventors again and again.

Stringfellow never stopped tinkering. In 1866 a group of enthusiasts founded the Aeronautical Society of Great Britain, one of the first organisations in the world devoted to the science of flight. Two years later, in 1868, the society held the world's first aeronautical exhibition, at the Crystal Palace, a giant glass-and-iron exhibition hall in London. Stringfellow, now almost 70, showed a model with three wings stacked one above another, a triplane, and won a prize of 100 pounds for a small steam engine with the best power for its weight. That prize sums up the whole problem of the time: everyone knew the challenge was to make an engine light enough for its power. John Stringfellow died in Chard in 1883, and the town's museum still remembers him as a pioneer of powered flight.

sections.heading: Downhill Hops in France and Russia
paragraphs: Models were one thing, but could a steam-powered machine carry a person? Two naval officers, one in France and one in Russia, decided to find out. Sailors knew a lot about wind, engines and how to build strong, light structures, so perhaps it is not surprising that they joined the race.

Félix du Temple de la Croix was a French naval officer born in 1823. With his brother Louis, he began by building large model airplanes in the 1850s. One model, said to weigh around 700 grams, was first powered by clockwork and later by a tiny steam engine. Both versions took off under their own power, flew a short distance and landed safely. In 1857 du Temple patented a design for a full-size monoplane with a tail and even a retractable undercarriage, wheels that could be folded away in flight, an idea far ahead of its time.

The full-size machine was built at Brest, a naval port in north-west France. It had a wingspan of about 13 metres and was made partly of aluminium, which was then a rare and expensive metal. Without its pilot, it weighed about 80 kilograms. Its engine used a clever steam boiler that du Temple designed himself, made of many thin tubes so it could heat water quickly while staying light. Later, the great American engineer Octave Chanute praised it as a very light steam boiler for its power.

Around 1874, with a person aboard, the machine was sent racing down a sloping ramp like a ski jump. It left the ground, travelled through the air for a very short distance, and came back down safely. It was not a real flight. The machine was not climbing on its own power, and the pilot could not steer it. But it is generally seen as the first time a full-size, engine-powered airplane carrying a person left the ground at all, a brief, powered hop.

Ten years later, in Russia, Alexander Mozhaysky tried something similar. Mozhaysky, born in 1825, was a Russian naval officer who had also built models and studied kites. In 1876 he began work on a full-size steam-powered monoplane. It had two small steam engines, which he had bought in England, driving three propellers. Around 1884, at a military field near St Petersburg, it was launched down a ramp with a mechanic aboard as pilot. It is said to have left the ground briefly before coming down, and one wing was damaged.

Decades later, during the Soviet era, some Russian books claimed that Mozhaysky had made the world's first powered flight. Russia's main aeronautics research institute, TsAGI, studied the claim carefully between 1971 and 1981. Its experts concluded that Mozhaysky's engines were much too weak to keep the plane flying. At best it made a short hop helped by the ramp. Even so, Mozhaysky deserves credit as a serious engineer whose ideas about propellers and controls were impressive for his time.

sections.heading: Clément Ader and the Bat-Winged Éole
paragraphs: Clément Ader was one of the most inventive engineers in France. Born in 1841, he first became famous not for flying but for sound. In 1878 he improved on Alexander Graham Bell's new telephone, and in 1880 he helped set up the telephone network in Paris. In 1881 he invented the 'théâtrophone', a system that sent live opera from the Paris Opera house through telephone lines to listeners about 3 kilometres away, with separate microphones for the left and right ear. It was the first stereo sound transmission in history.

But Ader's real passion was flight, and his inspiration came from a surprising animal: the bat. Bats are expert flyers, and their wings are made of thin skin stretched over long finger bones, which makes them light and flexible. Ader studied bats closely, and he designed a flying machine that looked like a giant one. He called it the Éole, after Aeolus, the god of the winds in Greek mythology.

The Éole had curved, bat-shaped wings about 14 metres across, made of silk stretched over a frame of light wood. At the front was a four-bladed propeller that looked a bit like the feathers of a huge bird. To power it, Ader built his own steam engine, and it was a little marvel: four cylinders, about 20 horsepower, and a weight of only about 51 kilograms. That was far lighter for its power than most steam engines of its day. With the pilot aboard, the whole machine weighed about 300 kilograms.

On 9 October 1890, on the grounds of a country estate at Armainvilliers, east of Paris, Ader climbed into the Éole and opened the steam valve. The propeller whirred, the machine rolled forward over flat ground, and then, according to the accepted account, it lifted off and travelled about 50 metres through the air at a height of roughly 20 centimetres, about the height of a shoebox, before settling back down. Only a few people were there to see it.

Historians give Ader real credit: the Éole was probably the first full-size, piloted airplane to leave flat ground under its own engine power, without a ramp or a downhill slope. But it was not a controlled flight. The Éole had no proper way for the pilot to steer it up and down or bank it from side to side. It stayed so close to the ground that it was probably being helped by 'ground effect', a cushion of air squeezed between a wing and the ground that gives extra lift when a wing flies very low. It could not climb higher, turn, or keep going.

Ader went on to build bigger machines for the French Army. His Avion III, with two steam engines of about 30 horsepower each and a wingspan of about 15 metres, was tested at Satory, near Versailles, in October 1897. On 14 October, a gust of wind pushed it off the circular track it was running on and damaged it. It did not fly. The army stopped paying for his work, and when its official reports were finally made public in 1910, they described the trials as unsuccessful. By then, Ader had begun claiming that he had made a long flight in 1897, but the evidence did not support him.

Ader did leave one lasting gift. He called his machines 'avions', from the Latin word 'avis', meaning bird. The name stuck. To this day, the ordinary French word for an airplane is 'avion', and people all over the French-speaking world say it every time they talk about flying.

sections.heading: Hiram Maxim's Giant on Rails
paragraphs: If anyone could solve the problem with sheer power, it should have been Hiram Maxim. Born in 1840 in Sangerville, Maine, in the United States, Maxim was a self-taught inventor who later moved to England. He is best known, sadly, for inventing the first fully automatic machine gun, the Maxim gun. He was rich, determined and confident, and in the early 1890s he decided to build a flying machine on a scale nobody had dared before.

At Baldwyn's Park, his home at Bexley in Kent, just south-east of London, he laid down a straight railway track about 550 metres (1,800 feet) long. On it he built an enormous test machine. It was about 12 metres long, with wings spanning over 30 metres, larger than the wings of many modern passenger jets. It is said to have had room for a crew of three. Two huge propellers, each about 5 metres (17 feet) across and made of layers of pine wood, were driven by two lightweight steam engines, often said to give about 360 horsepower together, burning naphtha, a light petroleum fuel, to heat the boilers quickly. With everything aboard, the machine weighed about 3.5 tonnes.

Maxim was a careful man, and he did not want the giant to fly away out of control. So it was not designed to fly freely. Instead, it ran on its rails, and four extra wheels on outrigger arms ran under a second set of wooden guard rails a few metres outside the main track. If the machine rose more than a few centimetres, these wheels would press up against the guard rails and hold it down. It was a test rig, a way to measure whether the wings could produce enough lift to raise such a heavy machine.

In 1894, on a run usually dated to 31 July, Maxim opened up the engines. The great propellers roared, steam hissed, and the machine charged down the track faster and faster. Then the wings did their job almost too well. The lift was so strong that the machine rose off its main rails and strained upward against the guard rails, until it tore part of them away. For a brief moment it was free in the air, perhaps a metre or less above the ground, before Maxim shut off the steam and it crashed back down, badly damaged.

Maxim had proven one important thing: wings really could lift a machine weighing several tonnes if you pushed them fast enough. But he had also shown how far there still was to go. His machine had no real way to be balanced or steered in free flight. And his steam plant, although astonishingly light for a steam engine, was still a heavy, complicated beast. Maxim concluded that a practical flying machine would need a lighter type of engine, such as one burning petrol.

He gave up the project, but he did not give up on flight entirely. He used what he had learned to design fairground rides in which passengers sat in little cars that swung outward as they spun around a tall tower, giving them a taste of flying. One of these 'Captive Flying Machines' opened at Blackpool Pleasure Beach in 1904, and visitors have been riding it for more than a century.

sections.heading: Lawrence Hargrave's Box Kites
paragraphs: While engineers in Europe and America were building huge, heavy machines, a quiet inventor on the other side of the world was taking a very different approach. Lawrence Hargrave was born in England in 1850 and moved to Australia as a teenager. He worked as an engineer and astronomer's assistant in Sydney, then gave up his job to spend his time studying flight.

Hargrave experimented with many things, including flapping models, rubber-powered models, and small engines powered by compressed air. He also worked on rotary engines, in which the cylinders spin around a fixed crankshaft; this type of engine later powered many early airplanes, although his own versions never became powerful enough for a full flying machine. But his most famous invention was much simpler. In 1893 he invented the box kite.

A box kite looks like two open-ended boxes joined by sticks, one at each end. The flat top and bottom surfaces of each box act like wings, stacked one above the other, while the side panels help keep the kite steady. Compared with ordinary flat kites, box kites made more lift for their size, produced less drag, and were remarkably stable. They did not need a tail and flew calmly even in strong winds.

On 12 November 1894, on the beach at Stanwell Park, south of Sydney, Hargrave tied four of his box kites together in a line, added a simple sling seat, and anchored the kite string through a spring balance to two heavy sandbags. With the help of a caretaker named James Swain, he let the kites rise in a wind of about 34 km/h (21 mph). Up went the kites, and up went Hargrave with them, about 4.9 metres (16 feet) into the air. He had been lifted off the ground by fixed wings with no gas, no hot air and no engine, just wind.

Hargrave's box-kite design proved that stacked, stable wings could carry a person, and it strongly influenced the next generation of builders. The box kite became one of the main ideas behind the biplane, an airplane with two wings stacked one above the other. Several early European airplanes of the 1900s looked very much like big box kites with engines attached. His work also inspired Alexander Graham Bell, who went on to experiment with giant kites built from many small triangle-shaped cells.

Hargrave also did something unusual: he refused to patent any of his inventions. He believed that ideas should be shared freely so that science could move faster, and he thought patent fees were a waste of money. 'Excellence of design and workmanship will always defy competition,' he wrote. Australia did not forget him. From 1966 to 1994, his portrait and drawings of his flying machines appeared on the back of the Australian 20-dollar note.

sections.heading: Langley's Aerodromes Over the Potomac
paragraphs: In the United States, one of the most respected scientists in the country was also working on the flying problem. Samuel Pierpont Langley was born in 1834 in Roxbury, Massachusetts. He became a famous astronomer, the first director of the Allegheny Observatory in Pittsburgh, where he studied the Sun. In 1887 he was made Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., which meant he was in charge of the nation's leading science museum and research organisation.

Langley began his flight research the scientific way. In 1887 he started building small rubber-band-powered models and gliders. At Allegheny he built a large whirling arm, much bigger and faster than Cayley's, to measure the forces on test surfaces at different speeds and angles. In 1891 he published his results in a book called 'Experiments in Aerodynamics'. He was convinced that powered flight was possible.

Then he began building models driven by tiny steam engines. He called them 'aerodromes', a word he made up from Greek roots meaning something like 'air runner'. His models had two pairs of wings, one behind the other (a design called tandem wings), a tail, and propellers driven by a lightweight steam engine of about one horsepower. Several early versions failed or broke, and his team spent years rebuilding and improving them.

Because the models could not take off from the ground, Langley launched them from a catapult on top of a houseboat floating on the Potomac River near Quantico, Virginia, about 50 kilometres south of Washington. Launching over water had an extra advantage: when a model came down, it landed on the river instead of smashing into the ground.

On 6 May 1896, Aerodrome No. 5 was flung off the catapult. It climbed, circled gently, and flew for about 90 seconds at about 40 km/h (25 mph), reaching heights of perhaps 25 to 30 metres before its fuel and water ran out and it settled softly onto the water. It was fished out, dried, and flown again the same day. Its two flights that day covered roughly 1,000 metres and 700 metres. Langley's friend Alexander Graham Bell, the inventor of the telephone, photographed the flight. Later that year, in November 1896, the slightly different Aerodrome No. 6 flew about 1.5 kilometres.

These were the first sustained flights by engine-powered, heavier-than-air machines of a decent size. They caused a sensation. But notice two things. First, there was nobody aboard. Second, nobody was steering. The models were carefully balanced so that they would fly steadily by themselves in calm air, but they simply went wherever the air and their own trim took them. A few years later, in 1898, the US War Department gave Langley 50,000 dollars to build a full-size Aerodrome that could carry a pilot. What happened to that machine in 1903 is a dramatic story that you will read in Part 8.

sections.heading: Power Was Not Enough
paragraphs: Let's step back and look at what sixty years of steam-powered experiments had achieved. Henson and Stringfellow designed a beautiful airliner that could never fly, and a small model that flew about 30 yards. Du Temple and Mozhaysky made short hops after racing down ramps. Ader's Éole skimmed about 50 metres just above the ground. Maxim's 3.5-tonne giant tore itself loose from its rails for a moment. Hargrave hung from kites on a beach. Langley's unmanned models flew about a kilometre over a river.

That is a lot of progress. These inventors proved that wings could lift heavy machines, that engines could drive propellers, and that a well-balanced model could fly steadily by itself. They designed lighter engines, better propellers and stronger structures. And they inspired thousands of people to believe that flight was coming.

But there was one thing none of them had solved. Not one of their machines could be properly CONTROLLED by a pilot in the air. Think about riding a bicycle. Having strong legs to push the pedals is not enough; you must also balance, lean into turns and steer, constantly making small corrections without even thinking about it. A flying machine is like a bicycle that can also tip forward and backward and slide sideways, all at once, in moving air full of gusts. Most of the steam inventors had concentrated on lifting and pushing. They hoped that once a machine was in the air, it would simply stay steady, or that they could work out the steering later.

There was also the engine problem. Steam engines, even the cleverest ones made by Ader, Maxim and Langley, were heavy, slow to start and needed water and fuel for their boilers. A new kind of engine, the petrol-burning internal combustion engine, was being developed for the first motor cars in the 1880s and 1890s. It would eventually be the key to powered flight, but it was not yet light and reliable enough.

So the next step did not come from a bigger engine at all. It came from someone who decided to forget about engines for a while and learn to fly like a bird, one careful glide at a time. In Germany, an engineer who had watched storks since he was a boy was building wings of cotton and willow and running down hills into the wind. His name was Otto Lilienthal, and he is the hero of Part 5.

deepDive: Why did steam fail as an aero engine, and how do historians judge the 'hop' claims? The core issue is specific power, the power an engine delivers per kilogram of total installed weight. A practical airplane of the 1900s needed something in the order of 1 horsepower for every 5 to 7 kilograms of engine, a figure steam struggled to approach once boilers, water and fuel were counted. Ader's 4-cylinder engine was remarkable on paper, about 20 horsepower for 51 kilograms of engine alone, but the full steam system weighed much more, and endurance was limited by water. Maxim got around this with brute force and naphtha burners, often given as about 360 horsepower in total on a 3.5-tonne rig, which showed that lift scales with wing area and the square of speed, yet his machine had essentially no flight control system. Historians also argue about definitions. For an aircraft to count as having truly flown, most aviation historians look for four things: it is piloted, it takes off under its own power (not just a ramp or slope), it sustains flight without losing height simply because of launch momentum, and the pilot can control it. By these tests, du Temple (about 1874) and Mozhaysky (about 1884) achieved ramp-assisted hops; Ader (1890) achieved a powered take-off from level ground but an uncontrolled, ground-effect hop of about 50 metres; Maxim (1894) proved lift on a restrained rig; and Langley (1896) achieved sustained but unpiloted and uncontrolled flight. Nationalist claims complicate the picture: Soviet-era publications promoted Mozhaysky until TsAGI's 1971–1981 study found his engines too weak, and Ader's later claim that Avion III had flown a long distance in 1897 was contradicted by the French Army's own report, published in 1910. Another debate concerns scaling. Stringfellow's 1848 model and Langley's 1896 aerodromes flew because small models have far more wing area per kilogram than full-size craft (the square-cube law). That is why successful models did not lead directly to successful piloted machines. Langley's full-size Great Aerodrome would show this painfully in 1903. The broad historical verdict is that this period solved structure and proved lift, while the decisive problems of control and a light, reliable internal-combustion engine were still waiting.
funFact: The everyday French word for airplane, 'avion', comes from the name Clément Ader gave his bat-winged steam flying machines in the 1890s.
